# Even the depth profile within a single integer fiber is not power-concave

This is an obstruction to a possible analytic regularity lemma, not to OC.
Let C be the convex pentagon with vertices

    (0,0), (3,0), (3,2), (2,4), (0,2).

Its integer fibers are [0,2], [0,3], [0,4], [0,2], respectively, and
its mixed length is M=11. Write f(t) for the unnormalized ambient
halfspace depth of (2,t).

For 12/5 <= t <= 13/5, the exact formula is

    f(t) = 9-3t   if t <= 5/2,
           4-t    if t >= 5/2.                       (1)

Here all ambient halfspaces are included. To prove (1), translate a
containing halfspace inward to its boundary through (2,t). If its continuous
normal is positive, write it as x >= t+a(z-2). The central fiber contributes
4-t. Fibers 1 and 3 contribute

    clamp(3-t+a,0,3) + clamp(2-t-a,0,2),

whose sum is at least max(5-2t,0). This follows by considering whether either
term saturates; in the unsaturated range their unclipped sum is 5-2t, and
each saturation value is greater than this nonnegative lower bound.
The fiber 0 contribution is nonnegative.

For t <= 5/2, choose a in [t-3,2-t]. Both terms are unsaturated, their
sum is 5-2t, and fiber 0 contributes zero. For t >= 5/2, choose a in
[2-t,t-3]. Both terms and the fiber 0 contribution vanish. Thus the upper
halfspaces attain the two values in (1). Halfspaces with negative continuous
normal contain a central-fiber segment of length at least t, which is larger
than either value in (1). Purely integer halfspaces containing (2,t) have
mass at least 6, and also cannot improve the minimum. This proves (1).

In particular,

    f(12/5)=9/5,   f(5/2)=3/2,   f(13/5)=7/5,

and (3/2)^2 < (9/5)(7/5). Thus log-concavity fails even on an actual
positive-volume integer fiber.

More strongly, no finite power-mean concavity holds. Fix any finite real p.
For small epsilon>0, let A=3/2. Formula (1) gives the two neighboring values
A+3 epsilon and A-epsilon. If p is nonzero, their average p-th powers equal

    A^p + p A^(p-1) epsilon + O(epsilon^2).

For p>0 this is greater than A^p, contradicting p-concavity at the midpoint.
For p<0 it is smaller than A^p, contradicting the reversed inequality
required by p-concavity. For p=0, the mean of the logarithms is
log(A)+epsilon/A+O(epsilon^2), again too large. Normalization by M does not
change any of these conclusions. Ordinary quasiconcavity of depth remains
valid; replacing it by a finite-power Brunn--Minkowski condition is invalid.
